The Las Vegas Community Ponds include fishing and stocking information for Cold Creek, Beatty, Floyd Lamb, Lorenzi, Sunset, and Veterans Memorial waters. These are Southern Nevada water in and around the Las Vegas Valley.

","pertinent_information":"

The following information is general, not specific, as some waters only get trout. Please check specific body of water to see stocking information. Water quality is generally good with spring flows helping to keep summer temperatures cooler. The primary game fish are rainbow trout and channel catfish, which are stocked seasonally. Other species include bluegill, green sunfish, crappie, and largemouth bass throughout city ponds. These latter species are not regularly stocked, but fish habitat placed in the pond provides cover for reproduction and recruitment. Small spinners, Power Bait, salmon eggs, and flies are effective for rainbow trout. Use spinner baits and rubber worms to catch largemouth bass. There is no overnight camping, but there are improved day use areas with restrooms, shade shelters, picnic tables, and barbecues. No fish parts are to be used or put into any community ponds.

This hot spot includes Floyd Lamb, Lorenzi, Sunset, Beatty, Hafen, and Boulder City Park ponds.

","fishing_report":"

Anglers continue to catch bluegill, bass and catfish throughout the day. Hotdog pieces and night crawlers are performing well for catfish as well as bluegill. A few bass have been caught on 3-inch craws and Ned rigs. As a reminder, no fish or fish parts may be used as bait in local park waters.

FLOYD LAMB STATE PARK POND

Hatchery also helps raise native nongame fish species found in southern Nevada. Warmwater species, including channel catfish, bluegill, wiper and tiger muskie, may also be obtained from other sources for stocking in Nevada waters.

Find the latest fishing reports and stocking updates here.

Fishing & Stocking Reports

Stay up to date with the latest fish stocking information and fishing reports from waters across Nevada.

Check Stocking UPDATES

Fishing Reports

Explore the latest fishing conditions across Nevada. NDOW fishing reports provide regular updates on waters throughout the state, including current conditions and recommended fishing spots by region.

View Latest Reports

Explore the Interactive FishNV Tool

Explore fishable waters across Nevada with the interactive FishNV map. Find lakes, reservoirs, streams and rivers, explore waters by fish species and plan your next fishing trip.

Pertinent Information

Topaz Lake is relatively large with a surface area of 2,410 acres, a length of 3.5 miles, a width of 1.5 miles, and maximum depth of 92 feet. Rainbow trout is the dominant sport fish, but bowcutt trout, brown trout, and occasionally tiger trout are stocked. Smallmouth bass and to a lesser degree largemouth bass are also popular for angling. Boaters should use a fish finder to determine the depth fish are occupying, which is usually in the upper 20 feet of the water column, and troll Rapalas or nightcrawlers with flashers to catch trout. Shore anglers do best with Power Bait or nightcrawlers and cast out as far as possible. The average size of rainbow trout is usually around 12 inches, but they commonly range from 10 to 18 inches. Several five pound or larger fish are caught every year. Black bass are commonly caught with rubber worms, jigs, and crankbaits along the shoreline or off deeper points. Most of the property around the lake is open to the public. Only portions of the west shore in Nevada and California and the far south end of the lake in California are private property. Boat launching is available at Topaz Marina and Douglas County Park. Douglas County Park provides camping, electrical hook-ups, bathrooms, picnic tables, playground, and a fish cleaning station. Topaz Marina has fishing boat rentals, boat slips, and food and drinks.

Western Region

Summer is here and fishing has been good in Western Nevada. The Truckee, Carson, and Walker Rivers are in great shape and have recovered fully from the intense thunderstorms that moved through recently. Temperatures have come up really quick in our rivers and will continue to increase as we really heat up. Early mornings will be the best time of day to find active trout until we start to cool off again. Our small streams have been fishing well and should provide some great hopper fishing until we see some extreme heat.

With Hobart closed to fishing and Marlette closed until July 17th, Spooner Lake is the only option to escape the heat for now. Be sure to check with the parks department before heading into the Hobart, Spooner, Marlette Wilderness. The northern Washoe county lakes have been good for trout and bass. Wall Canyon and Squaw Creek are both fishing well. Although they fished very well this spring, the Pine Forest reservoirs and lakes will start to slow down as we really heat up.

Many of the community ponds are still getting stocked but will slow down as conditions change. Marilyn’s Pond and Baily Pond will likely still receive plants through the end of June. As we really heat up, there’s always green sunfish to be caught in the Verdi Ponds and Baily Pond.

*Several western Nevada fisheries are under a Harmful Algae Bloom (HAB) warning. For the latest information on effected areas, visit The Nevada Division of Environmental Protection website

Stocking continues at bodies of waters across our area. Be sure to check the stocking report calendar for weekly updates.

Southern Region

LAKE MEAD — Anglers are reporting the most consistent striped bass action is taking place during the early morning hours and again at dusk. Stripers are biting on anchovies in the Hemenway area, with anglers averaging four fish in the 2– to 4-pound range. In Government Wash, anglers have found success when fishing in approximately 50 feet of water using shad-colored jigs and swimbaits worked off the bottom. Smallmouth bass are chasing minnow and flat worm plastics in shallow coves. With warmer temperatures forecasted for the weekend, the black bass bite is expected to improve.

LAKE MOHAVE / WILLOW BEACH — Anglers area catching rainbow trout ranging from 12 to 16 inches in length. Striped bass action remains slow near Willow Beach, with most catches reported by kayakers and boaters fishing deeper water with trout- and watermelon-colored soft baits. Similar conditions persist at the south end of the reservoir, where anglers are catching stripers of comparable size while fishing off the bottom at Telephone Cove. In Cottonwood Basin, bass are hitting soft plastics and jigs in olive and watermelon colors.

LAUGHLIN — Warmer temperatures are expected to increase fish activity along the river. Meanwhile, shore and dock anglers are catching both striped bass and rainbow trout. Stripers are showing a strong preference for anchovies and light-colored swimbaits. One angler reported landing an 11-pound striper on an anchovy just south of Casino Row. Rainbow trout are biting on yellow and olive jigs as well as a variety of spinners. The fish are also hitting on night crawlers.

LAS VEGAS COMMUNITY PONDS — The Nevada Department of Wildlife planted rainbow trout in the community fishing ponds. Stocked rainbows are taking worms, bright Rooster Tails and rainbow-colored PowerBait. Recent rains and snowfall have slowed catfish and bass activity. Anglers are reminded that city park limits are three fish per day and the use of fish or fish parts as bait is prohibited.

KIRCH WILDLIFE MANAGEMENT AREA — The water is still open with thin ice along the shorelines first thing in the morning. Anglers are catching trout on small jigs and Mouse Tails. Ice fishing is not possible.

In addition, the Nevada Division of State Parks (NDSP) has prohibited swimming for visitors and pets at the Silver Springs side of the reservoir due to elevated toxin levels. Stay out of the water!
